Houston Texans|Buffalo Bills.read: The model has Houston -3.5 while the market has Buffalo -1.5, a 5-point gap that spans the key numbers of 3 and 1. Almost none of it comes from availability: the home injury deltas (McDonald, Anderson-for-Hunter) sum to about -0.10 and the away deltas (Sanders, Johnson) to about -0.09, so injuries net to essentially zero and the market has nothing here it hasn't already priced. The entire disagreement sits in the base power ratings, where the model carries Houston at 3.65 and Buffalo at only 2.13, whereas the market clearly rates Buffalo as the better team by roughly a field goal on a neutral field. In Week 2 with limited new data, a rating gap that large against a strong, liquid market number is far more likely to be rating drift than a genuine mispricing, and the 1-star / 8.5% flag confirms the model itself has low conviction. Walters' rule applies: a big disagreement with no informational driver is a reason to audit the ratings, not to bet into them.
Houston Texans|Buffalo Bills.risks: If the Bills rating is genuinely stale (e.g., roster turnover the model hasn't caught) there could be real home value, but the trench units are roughly a wash and the 1.1-point total gap is well inside noise; main risk is chasing a phantom edge created by an underrated Buffalo.
Houston Texans|Buffalo Bills.recommendation_note: Lean home only if a rating audit confirms the Buffalo number.

Los Angeles Chargers|Arizona Cardinals.read: The model lands at 6.99 versus a market of 9.5, and essentially all of that 2.5-point gap comes from the base power ratings (0.86 vs -4.09 plus 2 HFA), not from injuries: the listed questionable tags are backups or negligible deltas (Leonard -0.02, Adams -0.06, Taylor-Demerson ~0) and net to almost nothing on either side. That means this is not an information edge from unpriced availability; it is a rating-level disagreement, likely the market grading Arizona lower (or the Chargers higher) than our numbers after Week 1 results, or our ratings drifting slowly. The 1-star flag (~7%) marks it as a genuine but small disagreement, and 2.5 points crossing 7 through 9 is a meaningful chunk of key numbers, which nudges toward the dog. Because the disagreement is rating-based rather than injury-based, treat it as a modest lean on Arizona +9.5 rather than a conviction play; if the market steps to 10 the value improves, if it drops toward 8 the edge is mostly gone.
Los Angeles Chargers|Arizona Cardinals.risks: The gap may reflect legitimate market information about Arizona's early-season form that the ratings have not yet absorbed (rating drift against us, not for us); the unit metrics show the Cardinals with weak rush efficiency and mediocre protection, so a Chargers blowout covering a big number is plausible. The O/U gap of 1.9 points is below actionable threshold. Line movement toward 8 would eliminate the edge.

Las Vegas Raiders|Miami Dolphins.read: The 2.6-point gap is almost entirely a power-rating disagreement, not injury information: the market's Raiders -3 implies Las Vegas is about a point better than Miami on a neutral field, while our ratings have Miami roughly a point better, a ~2-point spread in team quality that is classic early-season rating drift rather than something the market has missed. Brock Bowers being out is public and heavily reported, so the -0.6 delta is almost certainly already in the number; it pushes our line toward Miami but it is not an edge in itself. That leaves the bet resting on our ratings being more accurate than the market's on two mediocre teams two weeks into the season, which is thin. What makes it playable at all is the price: Miami +3 sits on the key number, and our number of Raiders -0.4 means we are getting more than 2.5 points of perceived value at the most common margin in the NFL. Treat this as a small position sized below the stated 2-star allocation, and only if +3 (or +3 -105 or better) is available; do not chase to +2.5.
Las Vegas Raiders|Miami Dolphins.risks: Rating drift could just as easily be on our side of the ledger; the market may correctly see a Raiders roster upgrade or a Dolphins regression our ratings have not caught yet. Bowers' absence also cuts Las Vegas' scoring ceiling, which argues against the mild 1.9-point over lean and reinforces staying off the total. If the line moves to +2.5 the key-number value evaporates and this becomes a pass.

Indianapolis Colts|Baltimore Ravens.read: The 5.3-point gap is almost entirely a base-rating disagreement, not an injury story: our power ratings have Baltimore only 0.3 better than Indianapolis on a neutral field, while the market has the Ravens roughly 5 points better, and the injury deltas barely move the needle (Madubuike OUT is -0.28 and Buchanan OUT is a wash, both already public and priced; Buckner/Campbell questionable tags are near-zero). Nothing on the report suggests information the market lacks, so this reads as rating drift on the Ravens/Colts side, likely stale Week 2 numbers that haven't caught up to how the market views both rosters. The 2-star flag simply measures that we disagree with a sharp number, and disagreeing with the market on team quality without an availability catalyst is not an edge under the Walters framework. If anything the lean is Colts at +3.3 with the Ravens' interior DL thinned, but the size of the gap argues for questioning our ratings rather than the market. Pass unless the Colts drift to +4 or worse, or a meaningful Ravens starter is downgraded.
Indianapolis Colts|Baltimore Ravens.risks: Our Colts and Ravens ratings may be stale or overfit to last season; Buckner sitting would further weaken an already poor Colts pass protection/interior matchup and could swing the game toward Baltimore; the OVER edge (2.6 pts) is modest and driven by the same ratings we're distrusting, so size it small.

Carolina Panthers|Chicago Bears.read: The 1.8-point gap is almost entirely a power-rating disagreement, not an availability story: the market prices Chicago roughly 5 points better than Carolina on a neutral field while our ratings have the gap at about 3, which reads as rating drift (Bears may be over-valued off narrative/QB expectations or Carolina under-valued) rather than information. The injury layer actually nets slightly toward the market, not away from it: Carolina losing Patrick Jones II (-0.46) is larger than the Bears' combined Odunze/Woods questionable tags (-0.27), so if anything the market may not yet have fully priced Jones out and the number could drift further toward Chicago. Bagent and Trapilo carry zero delta and the Q30 tags are coin-flip-ish, so there is no hidden availability edge on either side. At 1.5 stars (9.5%) this is below the actionable threshold in Walters' framework; the +3 on the home dog is a desirable key number to hold, but the edge is thin and rests on ratings we cannot independently verify against the market's information.
Carolina Panthers|Chicago Bears.risks: If the market moves to Bears -3.5 on Jones news, the +3 becomes a legitimate key-number buy for Carolina; conversely if Odunze and Woods are confirmed in, the small away deltas vanish and the model line drifts closer to -1.0, widening the gap on pure noise. Total gap of 1.6 (45.7 vs 47.3) is inside normal variance and not worth a position.

Cincinnati Bengals|Tampa Bay Buccaneers.read: The base line from ratings plus HFA is about +1.0 for Cincinnati, and the only injury input is Jonathan Allen at Q15 with a tiny -0.06 delta versus Slaton, so the model sits at 0.95 while the market has the Bengals at -3.5. That 2.5-point gap is not injury information -- Tampa is full strength and the Allen situation is nearly a wash -- so the disagreement is almost entirely a rating dispute: the market is treating Cincinnati as roughly a 3-point better team than our power numbers do, likely pricing offensive personnel or early-season perception that the ratings have not moved on. With no availability edge and a 1-star (8.5%) disagreement, this is a weak market-drift lean rather than a Walters-grade information play, but 2.5 points on a low-total NFL spread with the model getting the road team as a short dog is enough for a small position. The unit numbers show both teams below average in rushing and protection, with Tampa's protection markedly worse, which cuts slightly against the away side but is already in the ratings.
Cincinnati Bengals|Tampa Bay Buccaneers.risks: Rating drift may be ours, not the market's -- if Cincinnati's offense is stronger than the power number implies, the market is right and the edge evaporates; Allen's Q15 status could flip to out with negligible impact; small sample early-season ratings are the least reliable of the year; O/U gap of 0.5 is inside noise.

New York Giants|Dallas Cowboys.read: The entire 5.9-point gap is a power-rating disagreement, not an availability story: the model has the Giants roughly a point better than Dallas on a neutral field, while the market has Dallas about five better, and the injury deltas on both sides are essentially zero (Nabers Q -0.09, Cowboys losses all replacement-level). With no unpriced injury or QB information to explain a six-point rating split in Week 2, the likeliest cause is model drift or stale preseason ratings that have not absorbed what the market learned in Week 1. That makes this a noise-driven disagreement rather than an information edge, and the 3 stars should be read as a flag to audit the ratings, not as a reason to size up. The one structural positive is that home +3 catches the key number, so if a position is taken it should be small and on the Giants, but the Walters discipline is to pass when you cannot articulate what the market is missing. Unit metrics (Dallas rush edge vs. Giants protection edge) are already in the ratings and add nothing incremental.
New York Giants|Dallas Cowboys.risks: Ratings may be lagging Week 1 evidence or an unreported Giants QB/line situation that the market has priced; 48.3 total may already reflect a defensive or weather read the model lacks; a 4.7-point total gap with no supporting information carries the same drift risk as the side.

Minnesota Vikings|Green Bay Packers.read: The base rating gap (1.75 vs 0.18) plus 2 points of HFA already produces 3.57, so nearly all of the 1.9-point disagreement comes from the power ratings themselves, not from injuries; the injury deltas are tiny (home -0.03, away -0.29 net) and only nudge the line from 3.57 to 3.9. The market at Vikings -2 is effectively pricing Green Bay as the better team or a near pick-em, which means the disagreement is a rating dispute (drift or a model view on Minnesota that Vegas doesn't share), not withheld availability information. With only 1 star (7% edge) and no key number crossed between 2 and 3.9 in a meaningful way we can exploit at this price, this is noise-driven rather than information-driven. The O/U gap of 4.6 points (41.9 vs 46.5) is the stronger signal in the file, driven by both teams' weak pass-protection units and the Packers' offensive line questions, so the under carries more conviction than the side.
Minnesota Vikings|Green Bay Packers.risks: Divisional game with a young Vikings side means early-season power ratings are the least reliable they will be all year; if the market is right that Green Bay is the better team, laying more than a field goal in the model's view is a 2-point mistake. Zach Bako-Bewele (OT) status could swing the Packers' protection further, but that helps the side rather than the under only if it turns into turnovers. Under risk: Week 2 offenses and shootout variance in a dome, and the market total may already reflect scheme changes the model's ratings haven't caught.
